## Leviticus 27 – Notes

**Whole chapter**
- These are rules for gifts people chose to promise to God, not things the law required. Rich and poor could both keep their vows. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
- Vows weren't created by Moses. People already made them, and Moses regulated them. Nobody had to make a vow, but once made it had to be paid, either in kind or by its set money value. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-27.html
- Constable links this chapter to chapter 26: the blessings and curses were in a sense God's vows to Israel, and here are Israel's vows to God. People also tend to make vows during times of discipline. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-27.html
- The Expositor's Bible says the book seems complete at chapter 26. Some have suggested an editor moved this chapter from earlier in the book. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/27.htm

**v. 1–2**
- A "special vow" literally means to *separate* a vow. When someone vowed themselves or another person, the priest named the price for redeeming them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/27-2.html
- Gill says the word suggests something unusual or even "wonderful," made out of uncommon zeal. He also reports the Jewish view that "Israelites" excludes Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm
- An unnamed commentator: vowing a person meant paying their money value in place of the person. Another notes exceptions such as Nazirites and Levites, who served in person and couldn't be redeemed (1 Sam 1:11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/27-2.htm
- Guzik: the fixed price gave the vow a concrete action, which stopped empty promises. Not vowing was no sin (Deut 23:22), but a vow made had to be kept. He cites Peter-Contesse: Judges 11 and 1 Samuel 1 show a person could be dedicated to sanctuary service, and this law let them be released by payment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
- The Pulpit Commentary: a person in danger might vow themselves (Gen 28:20) or another (Judg 11:30; 1 Sam 1:11). Such vows were usually redeemed, Samuel being an exception. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-27.html

**v. 3–7**
- Guzik cites Rooker: the prices reflect either a worker's wage (about a shekel a month) or the value of the person's work at the tabernacle. Heavy labour explains why young men were valued highest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
- Gill:
  - 50 shekels was the highest valuation, and everyone of the same age paid the same, rich or poor.
  - The shekels had to be full weight by the sanctuary standard.
  - The gap between male and female values narrows in old age because their work is closer in value. He quotes a Jewish proverb that an old woman in a house is a treasure.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm
- Constable: what a person paid depended on the age and sex of the one pledged. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-27.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik: no one was shut out of vowing by poverty. God wanted dedication within everyone's reach. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
- Gill reports rabbinic rules: the priest was to leave a poor man enough to live on, such as a bed, his tools and his donkey (citing Rashi). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm
- The Pulpit homilies (Redford) see law and grace joined here: the law makes its claim, but God softens its harshness. They read this as a pointer toward the new covenant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/leviticus/27.htm
- The Biblical Illustrator reads it as a picture: Israel was "poorer than the estimation" at Sinai, and God's grace provides for that. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/leviticus-27.html

**v. 9–10**
- Gill: the rule blocked the trick of swapping in a worse animal while calling it better. Even an honest upgrade wasn't allowed. Maimonides says a man who swapped was beaten. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary: an animal fit for sacrifice couldn't be redeemed once vowed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-27.html

**v. 11–13**
- Guzik: an unclean animal, such as a donkey, could be given to the priest to use or sell. An owner who wanted to keep it paid its value plus a fifth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
- Constable: the priests probably used unclean animals for other work or sold them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-27.html
- Gill: anyone else could buy the animal at the priest's price, but the original owner had to add a fifth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm

**v. 14–15**
- Guzik: the house was valued, a fifth was added, and that total went to the tabernacle treasury. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
- An unnamed commentator: the extra fifth applies to the former owner (or, by later practice, his close relatives) because he is taking back something he promised to God. Matthew Poole adds that the fifth was bearable because priests usually set moderate prices. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/27-15.htm
- Gill: the fifth made people careful before vowing their property and made sure God got full value. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm

**v. 16**
- Gill: the verse says "part" of a field, so the family kept something to live on and land stayed in the family and tribe. The value was set by the amount of seed, not by how good the soil was. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary sees God checking excessive zeal here. It became a rule that no one should vow his whole estate and leave his family poor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-27.html
- Constable: inherited land that was vowed seems to have been paid for year by year. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-27.html

**v. 17–19**
- The price was reckoned against the years left until the Jubilee. The original owner could redeem at any time, or a close relative could do it for him (compare Lev 25). https://www.preceptaustin.org/kinsman-redeemer_-_the_goel
- The Pulpit Commentary: redeeming inherited land was the normal practice, and we never hear of priests building up landholdings this way. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-27.html

**v. 20–21**
- The Pulpit Commentary: if he had already sold his rights to the field until the Jubilee before vowing, he paid nothing, but the field passed to the sanctuary at the Jubilee. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/leviticus/27.htm
- Gill reports a Jewish commentator: if nobody redeemed the field, the priests paid fifty shekels and took it, and at the Jubilee it went to the priests as a body. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm

**v. 22–24**
- The Pulpit Commentary: for a purchased field the money was paid "in that day" as a lump sum, and the land went back to the original owner at the Jubilee. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-27.html
- Poole: no fifth was added here, because purchased land was held only until the Jubilee and was a weaker title than inherited land. Gill agrees and cites Maimonides. An unnamed commentator gives the reason for the different treatment: to push families or close relatives to redeem inherited land so it never left the family. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/27-23.htm
- Land returning at the Jubilee is part of the wider redeemer theme (Lev 25). https://www.preceptaustin.org/kinsman-redeemer_-_the_goel

**v. 26–27**
- Firstborn animals already belonged to God (Exod 13:2), so they couldn't be vowed. A clean firstborn had to be sacrificed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: a vow means going beyond what duty already requires. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-27.html
- **Commentators disagree on v. 27:**
  - Poole says it means the *firstborn* of an unclean animal, not unclean animals in general, since that would just repeat vv. 11–13.
  - Gill says it doesn't mean ordinary unclean firstlings, which were redeemed with a lamb. Following Rashi, he applies it to firstlings vowed for repairing the sanctuary.
  - Keil & Delitzsch say it does mean unclean firstborn. In their view it changes the earlier law (a donkey redeemed with a lamb or killed, Exod 13:13) in favour of the sanctuary's income.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/27-27.htm

**v. 28**
- Guzik: "devoting" something went further than a vow. It often meant destroying it, with all its value given to God, so it could never be bought back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
- **Disagreement over who could be devoted:**
  - One commentator says a man could ban his children and slaves.
  - Gill limits it to what was truly the man's own, meaning non-Israelite slaves. Citing a Jewish rule, he says children and Hebrew servants couldn't be devoted.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/27-28.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm
- Another commentator: applied to people, *chērem* (devoted) means only someone rightly condemned to death. This law doesn't approve rash vows like Saul's or Jephthah's, and devotion is different from sacrifice. Examples given are Hormah and Amalek's cattle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/27-28.htm
- Constable's examples: the spoil of Jericho, and a condemned murderer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-27.html

**v. 29**
- Guzik: no one could escape execution by being "bought back." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
- Gill: this means people doomed to destruction, such as idolaters, the Canaanite nations and Amalek, or those sentenced by judges. A master couldn't devote a servant to death; that would break the sixth commandment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm
- Unnamed commentators:
  - The ban may have applied only to notorious wrongdoers and been carried out by the community, not by individuals.
  - The text doesn't let a Jew devote his child to death, since murder was forbidden. This "peradventure was Jephthah's error."
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/27-29.htm
- The Pulpit homilies: this isn't about human sacrifice but justice on the wicked. Rash vows hurt the innocent (Jonathan, Jephthah's daughter). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/leviticus/27.htm
- The Expositor's Bible defends this as the rightful judgment of God as Israel's King. On the Canaanite cities, it argues their corruption was spreading along a major trade route. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/27.htm

**v. 30**
- Guzik: the Hebrew word for "tithe" is related to "ten." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: this law gave God's authority to an older custom (Gen 14:20; 28:22). Poole: this means the regular yearly tithe for the Levites. Gill: the tithe acknowledged God as owner of the land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/27-30.htm
- Gill explains the Jewish system: a first tithe for the Levites, a second tithe eaten in Jerusalem, and a poor tithe in years 3 and 6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm

**v. 31**
- Gill: this means one's own tithe. Redeeming a neighbour's tithe needed no extra fifth (citing Rashi). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/27.htm
- Cambridge Bible: crop and fruit tithes could be redeemed for the value plus a fifth, which sets them apart from animal tithes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/27-30.htm

**v. 32–33**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the animal tithe could not be redeemed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/leviticus/27.htm
- I found nothing on the shepherd's rod itself.

**v. 34**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the closing line of chapter 26 is repeated to show this chapter also belongs to the laws given at Sinai. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/leviticus/27.htm
- Guzik: these are real commandments, not suggestions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
- Constable quotes Goldberg: the Sinai laws began with ten commandments and end with ten laws about vows and tithes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-27.html

## Where Protestant teachers differ

I couldn't reach any denominational sites, so these are differences between the commentators I could read.

- **Tithing today (v. 30–33):**
  - Guzik: the New Testament doesn't command tithing, but giving should be in proportion to income (1 Cor 16:2), and 10% is a good place to start. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-27/
  - The Pulpit homilies treat the tithe (single or double) as a guide for regular giving. Special vows should come out of what's left after the tithe. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-27.html
- **Should Christians make vows?**
  - The Pulpit Commentary, which is Anglican, uses Church of England services as its examples of Christian vows: baptism and confirmation, marriage, ordination. It says a vow stops binding once a person is convinced it's wrong, and uses the vow of celibacy Luther and other Reformers broke as an example. Marriage vows are different, because they are also a promise to another person. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-27.html
  - The Expositor's Bible is more cautious. As far as the extract shows, it says vows are not forbidden now but not approved either. It argues Jesus' words in Matthew 15:5–6 don't prove vows are right today, since the old covenant was still in force then. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/27.htm
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary and the Biblical Illustrator say vows should be made carefully and usually with conditions. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-27.html
